amundsen-gjoa-006.description: The 47-ton square-sterned sloop Gjoa, 70 by 20 feet, built by Knut Johannesson Skaale at Rosendal in 1872 - the year Roald Amundsen was born - and a herring boat for twenty-eight years before Amundsen bought her from Asbjorn Sexe of Ullensvang on 28 March 1901. Photographed in 1903, before she sailed for the Northwest Passage. The photographer is very probably Anders Beer Wilse, whose 1903 photograph of the Gjoa is held by the Norsk Folkemuseum as Galleri NOR NF.W 22835; this copy differs in size from that one, so the match is probable rather than proved. Wilse died in 1949 and his work is public domain in Norway.

amundsen-gjoa-011.description: Adolf Henrik Lindstrom, the Gjoa's cook, holding a catch of fish at Gjoahavn (Uqsuqtuuq) in 1904. Fresh fish, seal and reindeer, not tinned stores, are why the Gjoa came through three Arctic winters without a case of scurvy, and Lindstrom went on to cook for Amundsen at Framheim in Antarctica.

amundsen-gjoa-019.description: The sloop Gjoa off the open Nome beach on the evening the passage ended, the Norwegian flag flying. The image is AL+CA 7747 in the University of Washington's Alaska, Western Canada and United States Collection; the local copy matches its dimensions and caption exactly.

amundsen-gjoa-020.description: Six of the Gjoa's men at Nome in September 1906. Gustav Juel Wiik had been buried at King Point on 9 May 1906 and Manni drowned at Qikiqtaruk (Herschel Island) later that summer. The photographer is unknown; the image is File:Nome Gjoa Amundsen.jpg on Wikimedia Commons and is public domain.

amundsen-gjoa-022.description: A map of the Gjoa's 1903-1906 route. No provenance is recorded for this copy, and the track artifact amundsen-gjoa-001, built from the dates in Roald Amundsen's own narrative, is the version to trust.

amundsen-gjoa-023.description: The Gjoa in her own building at the Fram Museum on Bygdoy in Oslo, where the ship has stood since she was returned to Norway in 1972. Photographed in 2017. The file is marked all rights reserved by the Fram Museum (storm@frammuseum.no) and must not be republished without permission.

amundsen-gjoa-024.description: The hamlet of Uqsuqtuuq (Gjoa Haven) on the harbour where Roald Amundsen's Gjoa wintered from September 1903 to August 1905, photographed on 20 February 2014. About 1,350 people live here; it is the only settlement on King William Island.

amundsen-gjoa-025.description: The Nattilik Heritage Centre at Uqsuqtuuq (Gjoa Haven), the community's own museum and cultural centre, opened in 2013. It holds the Netsilik side of this history and material from the Franklin searches. Photographed 7 September 2019.

amundsen-gjoa-026.description: CCGS Amundsen, the Canadian Coast Guard medium icebreaker named for Roald Amundsen, on the St Lawrence between Quebec City and Levis on 8 March 2011. Launched in 1978 as the Sir John Franklin, laid up in 2000, converted at Les Mechins and recommissioned as CCGS Amundsen on 26 August 2003 as a dedicated Arctic research vessel - ninety-eight years to the day after the Gjoa met the Charles Hanson off Nelson Head. She is the ship this dashboard runs on.

amundsen-gjoa-031.description: Roald Amundsen on the death of Gustav Juel Wiik at King Point on 31 March 1906: "At about 5 p.m. ... the bell rang very loudly, all of a sudden. There was something in the ring that spelt disaster, and I ran off at full speed. But I was only just in time to see our dear friend breathe his last. It was an inexpressibly sad moment. I closed the eyes of our late comrade, and we remained sitting there for a while in silence and sorrow."

amundsen-gjoa-032.description: Roald Amundsen on Netsilik winter clothing, written on the sledge journey of 1 March 1904 at 63 degrees below zero: "My experience is that the Eskimo dress in winter in these regions is far superior to our European clothes. But one must either wear it all or not at all; any mixture is bad. Woollen underclothing absorbs all the perspiration and soon becomes wet through and through."

amundsen-gjoa-034.description: The crew cut the fringes off their new caribou anoraks, thinking them ridiculous on grown men. Roald Amundsen did not: "But I had my scruples about this, as I had already had evidence that nothing either in the Eskimo's clothing or other arrangements was, in fact, without meaning or purpose, so I kept my fringe and put up with the ridicule." The trimmed anoraks began to curl up like neckties and the fringes went back on.

amundsen-gjoa-036.description: The scanned page images of volume I of Roald Amundsen's The North West Passage, 22.8 MB, as printed by Archibald Constable in 1908: the plates, the folding route chart and the printed spellings of the Netsilik names, none of which survive intact in the OCR text (amundsen-gjoa-003). The printed page is the authority for any quotation or name from this volume.

amundsen-gjoa-039.title: Roald Amundsen: the frontispiece portrait, signed
amundsen-gjoa-039.description: The photogravure portrait of Roald Amundsen that faces the title page of volume I of The North West Passage, with his signature reproduced beneath it. He was thirty-four when the Gjoa reached Nome on 31 August 1906.

amundsen-gjoa-040.description: A measured diagram of the Gjoa captioned 'Deck of the "Gjoa"': her sail plan above and a deck plan below, keyed a. Aft Cabin, b. Engine Room, c. Main Hold, d. Fore Cabin, with the note '"Gjoa" (47 tons R.)'. It is the clearest single statement of what Roald Amundsen's ship actually was - a 47-ton herring sloop with a 13-horsepower paraffin motor and seven men aboard.

amundsen-gjoa-044.title: The fire in the engine room
amundsen-gjoa-044.description: The plate Roald Amundsen captions simply 'The Fire': the engine-room fire aboard the Gjoa on the night of 31 August 1903, in the shoal water east of King William Land, among tanks holding 2,200 gallons of petroleum. Gustav Juel Wiik stayed at his post below; two extinguishers and hand pumping put it out.

amundsen-gjoa-049.description: Men and dogs drawn up on the ice at the start of the expedition's first sledge journey out of Gjoahavn (Uqsuqtuuq) in March 1904. The printed plate letters three of them by name: Roald Amundsen, Helmer Hansen and Lieutenant Godfred Hansen.

amundsen-gjoa-051.description: A young Netsilik man drawing a bow, photographed against the snow. Roald Amundsen calls him 'the Owl' throughout the narrative - Ugpi or Uglen - and employed him from June 1904 on the magnetic and surveying journeys; he became, Amundsen writes, an exceptionally clever hunter of birds and reindeer. He was about thirty and married to Kabloka. Most of the Netsilingmiut appear in the book under nicknames the Norwegians gave them, and their own names in modern Inuktitut orthography are not yet recorded here.

amundsen-gjoa-053.description: A group of people in a snow house. Roald Amundsen's printed caption is 'Umiktuallu Kills his Foster-son', and the plate is one of the very few in the book tied to an event in the internal life of the Netsilik community at Gjoahavn rather than to the expedition. What the caption asserts is Amundsen's account, made by a European visitor in 1904 and published in 1908; it is not the community's own telling, and should be read with that in mind. Umiktuallu was the elder brother of Ugpi, married to Onallu, and the same man who a year later was paid a file and an old knife for his foster-son Manni when Manni joined the ship.

amundsen-gjoa-055.title: Netsilingmiut paying a visit to the Gjoa: Anana, Onaller, Kabloka and Umiktuallu
amundsen-gjoa-055.description: A loaded sledge and dog team drawn up on the sea ice with a group standing beside it, captioned 'Nechilli Eskimo paying a visit'. Four of the party are lettered by name above the picture: Anana, Onaller, Kabloka and Umiktuallu - Ugpi's mother, Umiktuallu's wife, Ugpi's wife and Umiktuallu himself. Netsilingmiut families camped beside the Gjoa through both winters at Gjoahavn (Uqsuqtuuq) and this is one of the few plates in volume I in which the sitters are named.

amundsen-gjoa-056.title: A Netsilik winter camp, photographed by moonlight
amundsen-gjoa-056.description: Snow houses on the sea ice at night, captioned by Roald Amundsen 'An Eskimo camp in winter time' and marked on the plate 'Photograph taken by moonlight'. It is a technically remarkable exposure for 1904-05 and the fullest published view of how the Netsilingmiut wintered beside the Gjoa at Gjoahavn (Uqsuqtuuq).

amundsen-gjoa-057.description: The hut the expedition called Uranienborg, built ashore at Gjoahavn (Uqsuqtuuq) to house the astronomical instruments, photographed in the winter dark; the leaf carries a second, smaller view lettered 'Assistent's compartment'. Godfred Hansen, the expedition's astronomer, wanted it built as a rotunda, so the crew built him a snow house, and an empty barrel served as the instrument pier. The magnetic observatories stood on the same ground, and determining the position and movement of the North Magnetic Pole was the stated purpose of the whole voyage.

amundsen-gjoa-060.title: Nalungia and Atikleura outside their tent
amundsen-gjoa-060.description: Nalungia and Atikleura standing with their family outside their skin tent, named in the printed caption. Atikleura is the man whose snow-house building Roald Amundsen describes at length in volume II, block by block, and Nalungia is the woman who worked the loose snow 'as fine as grated sugar' and chinked every crevice from outside while he set the blocks from within. The technique went straight into the expedition's second magnetic observatory, a large igloo with ice windows.

amundsen-gjoa-062.description: The contents of volume I of Roald Amundsen's The North West Passage and, on the three leaves that follow, its full list of illustrations with the page each plate faces - the key to every plate in the volume, including the magnetic instruments, the observatory views and the portraits of the Netsilingmiut. The three illustration pages are registered separately as amundsen-gjoa-063, -064 and -065.

amundsen-gjoa-063.pages: vol. I, list of illustrations, p. xi
amundsen-gjoa-063.description: The first page of the printed list of illustrations for volume I of The North West Passage, plate by plate with the page each faces. It names, among much else, the magnetic instruments, the self-registering magnetic variation apparatus, the observatory for the absolute magnetic observations, the plates of the Netsilingmiut, and the chart of the Gjoa's route through the North West Passage bound at the end of the volume.

amundsen-gjoa-064.pages: vol. I, list of illustrations, p. xii
amundsen-gjoa-064.description: The second page of the printed list of illustrations for volume I of The North West Passage. It runs from the Villa Magnet and Uranienborg through the first Christmas Eve on board and the first sledge expedition to the portraits of Kabloka, Umiktuallu, Onaller and Talurnakto, Adolf Lindstrom with his fish, and the Netsilik graves.

amundsen-gjoa-065.pages: vol. I, list of illustrations, p. xiii
amundsen-gjoa-065.description: The third page of the printed list of illustrations for volume I of The North West Passage: from 'A Hunting Party' through Uranienborg in winter, the snow huts in the Lindstrom Valley, Magito, Nalungia and Atikleura outside their tent, and the Netsilik implements, ending with the chart of the Gjoa's route bound at the end of the volume.

amundsen-gjoa-066.description: The frontispiece of volume II of The North West Passage: the Gjoa's first meeting with whalers after completing the passage. In Roald Amundsen's telling this was 26 August 1905, off Nelson Head, when the Gjoa met the San Francisco whaling schooner Charles Hanson, Captain James McKenna, working east out of the Pacific - proof of continuous navigable water from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

amundsen-gjoa-067.description: Praederik and his wife photographed by lamplight inside their snow house, named in the printed caption. Praederik was an angakkuq; Roald Amundsen describes his work as conjuring and sorcery, which is what a European in 1908 made of it.

amundsen-gjoa-068.title: Netsilingmiut visitors on board the Gjoa
amundsen-gjoa-068.description: A long line of men, women and children standing beside the ship, captioned 'Nechilli Eskimo visitors on board'. Netsilingmiut families visited the Gjoa constantly through both winters at Gjoahavn (Uqsuqtuuq); Roald Amundsen records taking as many as thirteen guests to sleep on his cabin floor on cold nights.

amundsen-gjoa-069.title: Scene on deck, summer 1904
amundsen-gjoa-069.description: Netsilingmiut and the Gjoa's crew standing together on the ship's deck in the summer of 1904, between the expedition's two winters at Gjoahavn (Uqsuqtuuq). The printed caption is 'Scene on deck. (Summer, 1904)'.

amundsen-gjoa-070.title: Festivities in the cabin: Godfred Hansen, Gustav Wiik and Anton Lund
amundsen-gjoa-070.description: Three of the Gjoa's men at a party in the ship's cabin, lettered by name in the printed plate: Godfred Hansen, Gustav Wiik and Anton Lund. Named portraits of the crew are rare in these volumes, and this is one of a pair on consecutive pages. Wiik died at King Point on 31 March 1906 and did not come home.

amundsen-gjoa-071.title: Festivities in the cabin: Roald Amundsen, Helmer Hansen and Peder Ristvedt
amundsen-gjoa-071.description: The second of the pair of named cabin portraits: Roald Amundsen, Helmer Hansen and Peder Ristvedt round the cabin table, with framed photographs on the bulkhead behind them.

amundsen-gjoa-073.title: An Ichyuachtorvik man in his kayak
amundsen-gjoa-073.description: A kayaker on open water, captioned 'Ichyuachtorvik Eskimo in his kayak'. Ichyuachtorvik is Roald Amundsen's spelling for the district north of Gjoahavn (Uqsuqtuuq) from which several of the people named in the narrative came.

amundsen-gjoa-074.title: The wrecked whaler Bonanza at King Point
amundsen-gjoa-074.description: The San Francisco whaling schooner Bonanza lying wrecked at King Point on the Yukon coast, with the Gjoa and the expedition's house beyond her; the plate letters all three - 'Bonanza', 'Gjoa', 'Our Residence'. The Bonanza had been run ashore days before the Gjoa arrived on 3 September 1905, and her second mate, the Norwegian Christian Sten, rowed out to meet the ship.

amundsen-gjoa-075.title: In winter quarters at King Point
amundsen-gjoa-075.description: The Gjoa and the huts at King Point on the Yukon coast in the third winter, 1905-06, masts and rigging along the shore. Twenty people wintered here together: the Gjoa's Norwegians, the Norwegian Christian Sten of the wrecked whaler Bonanza with his wife Kataksina and their small daughter, and the Inuvialuit families of Jimmy, Neiu and Kunak.

amundsen-gjoa-076.title: Kunak and his family, summer at King Point
amundsen-gjoa-076.description: Kunak with his family outside their tent at King Point in the summer of 1906, his name lettered on the plate. Kunak built his house alongside Christian Sten's for the winter of 1905-06, and he and his family came aboard the wreck of the Bonanza to see the Gjoa off when she finally got away in July 1906.

amundsen-gjoa-077.title: The American whaling fleet at Herschel Island, 1905-1906
amundsen-gjoa-077.description: The American whaling fleet lying at Qikiqtaruk (Herschel Island) in the winter of 1905-06, masts and rigging along the ice. Several hundred people wintered at the station - whaling crews, Inuvialuit families and, for part of the winter, the Gjoa's men. Roald Amundsen walked over from King Point in October 1905 on his way to the telegraph at Eagle.

amundsen-gjoa-079.title: An Inuvialuit tent at King Point
amundsen-gjoa-079.description: A skin tent pitched on the shore at King Point with a family and their dogs beside it, captioned 'Eskimo tent at King Point'. Inuvialuit families wintered alongside the Gjoa's people here in 1905-06, and Roald Amundsen's men depended on them for fresh meat, sewing and guiding.

amundsen-gjoa-081.title: Manichya and family at King Point
amundsen-gjoa-081.description: Manichya with his family in fur clothing at King Point, named in the printed caption. When Manni, the young Netsilingmiut who had joined the Gjoa at Gjoahavn (Uqsuqtuuq), asked in the spring of 1906 to live among Inuit again, it was Manichya who took him in; Manni came back to the ship weeks later hollow-cheeked and thin, and Roald Amundsen took him aboard again.

amundsen-gjoa-082.title: Fort Egbert, near Eagle City, Alaska
amundsen-gjoa-082.description: The line of buildings at Fort Egbert on the Yukon River near Eagle City, Alaska, held in 1905 by two companies of the US 3rd Infantry. Roald Amundsen drove in off the river ice in early December 1905 after some 800 km on ski, snowshoe and dog sledge from King Point, and sent from the telegraph office inside this fort the message that the Northwest Passage had been sailed. It went, he wrote, only just in time: the wires came down shortly afterwards in the cold.

amundsen-gjoa-084.title: After our arrival at Nome
amundsen-gjoa-084.description: A group photographed after the Gjoa reached Nome on 31 August 1906, the sitters lettered with their names in the plate, Roald Amundsen among them. It is the end of the voyage: three years and two and a half months out of Christiania.

amundsen-gjoa-085.title: Sports at Nome
amundsen-gjoa-085.description: A ski jumper in mid-air above a snow-covered slope at Nome, with spectators along a scaffold below - captioned simply 'Sports at Nome'. The Gjoa anchored off Nome on 31 August 1906, so the snow in this plate belongs to the winter that followed rather than to the arrival.

amundsen-gjoa-087.description: The contents of volume II of The North West Passage and, on the three leaves after it, the full list of illustrations with the page each plate faces. The list is what identifies the plates in this volume, several of which are otherwise indistinguishable - Wiik's grave, the coffee party at King Point, the register house, the tattooed arm and thigh, Jimmy and Kappa on the mail trip, the graves and huts at Qikiqtaruk (Herschel Island). It ends with the chart of King Haakon VII's Coast and Queen Maud's Sea from Godfred Hansen and Peder Ristvedt's sledge expedition of 1905, bound at the end of the volume. The three illustration pages are registered separately as amundsen-gjoa-088, -089 and -090.

amundsen-gjoa-088.pages: vol. II, list of illustrations, p. vii
amundsen-gjoa-088.description: The first page of the printed list of illustrations for volume II of The North West Passage, plate by plate with the page each faces: from the frontispiece of the Gjoa's first meeting with whalers through the Netsilik chapters to the wrecked Bonanza and the houses at King Point.

amundsen-gjoa-089.pages: vol. II, list of illustrations, p. viii
amundsen-gjoa-089.description: The second page of the printed list of illustrations for volume II: Kunak and his family, the American whaling fleet and the theatrical performance at Qikiqtaruk (Herschel Island), Gustav Wiik in the winter of 1905, Wiik's grave at King Point, Anakto, Manichya and family, Fort Egbert near Eagle City, Jimmy and Kappa who took part in the mail trip, and Tupsi.

amundsen-gjoa-090.pages: vol. II, list of illustrations, p. ix
amundsen-gjoa-090.description: The third page of the printed list of illustrations for volume II: Manni in the summer of 1906, Anton Lund, the arrival at Nome, the sports at Nome, the Gjoa at anchor off Nome, Godfred Hansen and Peder Ristvedt in the spring of 1906, and the dogs; it ends with the chart of King Haakon VII's Coast and Queen Maud's Sea from Hansen and Ristvedt's sledge expedition of 1905.
